briefs.copd:
Obstructive Lung Disease

asthma vs COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) by spirometry · alpha-1 antitrypsin · what lowers COPD mortality · long-term oxygenIs the obstruction reversible, and does the intervention change survival or only symptoms?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Reversibility is a measurement: spirometry before and after a bronchodilator separates asthma from COPD; relief after albuterol does not.

  • Asthma: FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) rises 12% or more and 200 mL or more; the ratio often normalizes.
  • COPD: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC (forced vital capacity) below 0.70; obstruction persists despite some improvement.
  • Asthma-COPD overlap: long-standing asthma, smoking, fixed obstruction; include an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS).

In COPD, rank interventions by outcome. These lower mortality:

  • Smoking cessation: first-line while the patient still smokes.
  • Long-term oxygen: for resting hypoxemia that meets the criteria below.
  • Others: annual influenza vaccination; lung volume reduction surgery in severe upper-lobe emphysema with low exercise capacity; nocturnal noninvasive ventilation for chronic daytime hypercapnia.

Bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, macrolides and roflumilast reduce symptoms or exacerbations, with no survival benefit shown as single additions; the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) cites triple-therapy data, not verified here ⚠︎. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves dyspnea, fatigue and quality of life.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Asthma – onset in childhood or early adulthood; episodic, variable, trigger-driven, often atopic; reversible obstruction · COPD – progressive, usually after 40 and years of smoking; post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 · Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency – emphysema in the young or minimal smoker, panlobular and worst at the bases; liver disease from misfolded protein: neonatal cholestasis, later cirrhosis
Management and treatment
Long-term oxygen: who qualifies
ThresholdApplies whenThen
PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) 55 mm Hg or less, or SaO2 (arterial oxygen saturation) 88% or lessAt rest; not for exertional or nocturnal hypoxemia aloneOxygen 15 hours a day or more, titrated to SaO2 90 to 94%
PaO2 59 mm Hg or less, or SaO2 89% or lessWith cor pulmonale or secondary polycythemia (hematocrit over 55%)Oxygen; reversing hypoxic vasoconstriction protects the right heart
By diagnosis Asthma – inhaled corticosteroid, with or without a long-acting beta-agonist · COPD – long-acting muscarinic antagonist and beta-agonist; add an inhaled corticosteroid for frequent exacerbations with eosinophils of 300/μL or more · Secondary polycythemia – treat the hypoxemia, not the number; phlebotomy only for symptomatic hyperviscosity, typically hematocrit over 65% · Polycythemia vera – all three cell lines up, low erythropoietin, a JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) mutation
Practice
  1. 68-year-old man with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is seen for follow-up former smoker, quit 2 years ago already on a long-acting bronchodilator pair No ankle edema PaO2 52 mm Hg at rest on room air · hematocrit 46% → Long-term oxygen therapy → a resting PaO2 of 55 mm Hg or less meets the standard criterion: long-term oxygen, which lowers mortality
  2. 68-year-old man with COPD asks what else reduces mortality stopped smoking 3 years ago already completed pulmonary rehabilitation and is vaccinated Dyspnea on one flight of stairs SaO2 87% at rest on room air · hematocrit 49% → Long-term oxygen if hypoxemic → with cessation already done, long-term oxygen for resting hypoxemia is a remaining intervention that lowers mortality; bronchodilators and roflumilast treat symptoms
  3. 68-year-old man with stable COPD has ankle edema from cor pulmonale jugular venous distension, loud pulmonic second sound ruddy, plethoric face PaO2 57 mm Hg at rest · SaO2 89% · hematocrit 57% · white cells and platelets normal → Start long-term oxygen → cor pulmonale or a hematocrit over 55% lowers the gate to PaO2 59 mm Hg or SaO2 89%: start oxygen now
  4. 68-year-old man with COPD still smokes a pack a day two exacerbations this year asks which single step most improves survival No oxygen requirement SaO2 93% at rest · FEV1 48% of predicted → Smoking cessation → smoking cessation gives the largest mortality benefit available; oxygen is for resting hypoxemia, which he lacks
  5. 68-year-old man with COPD is referred to pulmonary rehabilitation asks what it will achieve breathless walking to the mailbox Stopped smoking last year SaO2 92% at rest · FEV1 45% of predicted → Improved symptoms and quality of life → rehabilitation improves dyspnea, fatigue and quality of life; it does not raise lung function
  6. 68-year-old man with COPD has had 3 exacerbations this year on a long-acting bronchodilator pair for 2 years inhaler technique and adherence checked Former smoker SaO2 93% at rest · blood eosinophils 340/μL → Add an inhaled corticosteroid → eosinophils of 300/μL or more with frequent exacerbations: adding an inhaled corticosteroid reduces exacerbations
  7. 24-year-old woman has 6 months of episodic wheeze and cough worse with exercise and cold air symptom-free between episodes Spirometry today is normal Afebrile · SaO2 98% · lungs clear on exam → Methacholine challenge → suspected asthma with normal spirometry: methacholine challenge; a negative test rules out asthma
  8. 62-year-old man has 3 years of progressive exertional dyspnea 40 pack-years of smoking daily cough with sputum No childhood wheeze or allergies Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.62 · FEV1 up 6% after albuterol → COPD → a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 with little reversibility is COPD: a long-acting muscarinic antagonist and beta-agonist
  9. 30-year-old woman has episodic wheeze and chest tightness each spring eczema as a child; hay fever never smoked Symptom-free between episodes Afebrile · pre-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.66 · post 0.78, FEV1 up 18% and 350 mL → Asthma → a 12% and 200 mL rise with a normalized ratio is reversible obstruction: asthma, treated with an inhaled corticosteroid
  10. 40-year-old man has 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnea minimal smoking history: 5 pack-years, quit at 25 CT: emphysema worst in the lower lobes Mildly raised liver enzymes Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58 → Alpha-1 antitrypsin level → emphysema under about 45, little smoking, lower lobes, and liver involvement: alpha-1 antitrypsin level
  11. 34-year-old woman with asthma has worsening control despite high-dose inhalers coughs up brown mucus plugs most mornings CT: central bronchiectasis Aspergillus precipitins positive; skin test to Aspergillus positive Afebrile · eosinophils 1,400/μL · IgE 2,600 international units per mL → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → refractory asthma with brown plugs and central bronchiectasis is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA): oral steroids and itraconazole
  12. 70-year-old woman with COPD has had 2 hospitalized exacerbations this year on a long-acting bronchodilator pair uses her inhalers correctly Quit smoking 10 years ago SaO2 92% at rest · blood eosinophils 360/μL → Add ICS → frequent exacerbations with eosinophils of 300/μL or more: add an inhaled corticosteroid
  13. 29-year-old man has 3 months of dry cough worse at night and when he runs in cold air no heartburn; takes no medications Never smoked; no postnasal drip Afebrile · spirometry normal · chest x-ray normal → Cough-variant asthma → isolated cough worse at night and with cold air and normal spirometry is cough-variant asthma
  14. 55-year-old woman, a long-standing asthmatic who smokes, is breathless breathless on most days for a year, not only in attacks obstruction no longer fully reverses Prior inhaled corticosteroid response Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.64 · FEV1 up 9% → Asthma-COPD overlap → long-standing asthma with smoking and fixed obstruction is asthma-COPD overlap; the regimen must include an inhaled corticosteroid
  15. 60-year-old man, a smoker, has chronic airflow obstruction productive cough for years and progressive dyspnea barrel chest The team must decide between emphysema and chronic bronchitis as the main process Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.60 → DLCO → the diffusing capacity (DLCO) is low in emphysema, normal in chronic bronchitis, and normal or high in asthma
  16. 15-year-old boy has had a wet cough since infancy recurrent sinusitis and two pneumonias digital clubbing; weight below the 5th percentile Never smoked; eats well but stays thin Afebrile · SaO2 94% · chest x-ray: hyperinflation → Cystic fibrosis → clubbing with a lifelong wet cough and poor growth points to cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride test; clubbing is not a feature of COPD or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
How NBME framed it: question 1

16-year-old girl in the emergency department with 3 days of cough with thick yellowish sputum and 1 day of shortness of breath No fever. Asthma on albuterol and inhaled corticosteroids, hospitalized 10 times between ages 8 and 10 Smokes 1.5 packs a day for 4 years T 37 °C · pulse 102/min · respirations 42/min · BP 108/80 mm Hg mild clubbing; increased anteroposterior chest diameter; occasional end-expiratory wheezes chest x-ray: severe bilateral hyperinflation, nothing else

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Congenital lobar emphysema: emphysema and hyperinflation; but it overinflates one lobe, not both lungs diffusely, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is more common.
  • Kartagener syndrome: thick sputum and clubbing; but there is no situs inversus, chronic sinusitis or lifelong wet cough.
  • Pulmonary sequestration: a congenital lung lesion; but it gives recurrent pneumonia in one region, and this film shows only hyperinflation.
  • Sarcoidosis: chronic lung disease in the young; but there is no hilar adenopathy or infiltrate.

Down to two: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or Kartagener syndrome. Emphysema this young, with barrel chest and diffuse hyperinflation, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: unopposed neutrophil elastase, panlobular and basal; misfolded protein in the liver causes cirrhosis. The common answer (severe asthma in a smoker) is not offered, the childhood asthma admissions pull toward it, and the clubbing is a planted pull toward Kartagener syndrome. Confirm with a serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level.

Pairs with Asthma covers severity and step therapy once asthma is confirmed. Recurrent Sinopulmonary Infection covers ABPA and the structural lung. Ask: which test measures the defining variable?
Transferable rule

When two choices test the same variable, pick the one that yields a number. An association is not a discriminator, and an intervention is ranked by the outcome the question names.
